summary: Aerospace engineers designing a spacecraft, station, Moon base or pressurized rover need to know which of NASA's microgravity fire experiments were actually run in an atmosphere like theirs. Our dashboard ranks the 19 PSI combustion investigations named in the challenge by how closely their tested oxygen and pressure match a chosen habitat, using each investigation's own PSI experimental table. It names the single test closest to the habitat's air and shows where the evidence stops. For the planned Moon base (30% O2, 10.2 psi), FLEX test #41 ran at 30% O2 and 10.3 psia, while the BASS-II and Saffire solid-material fire tests stopped about 8 oxygen points short.
details: What it does: an aerospace engineer picks a habitat (spacecraft, space station, Moon base, pressurized rover or Mars base). Its oxygen and pressure come from a quoted source: the challenge statement for the Moon base and pressurized rover (30% O2 or more at 10.2 psi or less; we check the boundary values), and the PSI-20 description for spacecraft and stations (14.7 psia, 21% O2). The challenge gives no Mars base atmosphere, so the engineer enters one. Any value can be edited. For each of the 19 PSI combustion investigations named in the challenge, the page shows: the O2 and pressure range found in its PSI experimental table, with the file name, and whether the habitat's value is inside the range or how far away it is; the single test closest to the habitat on both values together, counting only oxygen-nitrogen atmospheres (FLEX also ran CO2 and helium suppression tests, which are left out and counted); "not in PSI table" where a table has no such column, instead of a guess; values stated only in a PSI description, labelled as such and quoted (ACME BRE); and descriptions that contradict themselves, shown with both quotes and not ranked (CFI's pressure range). Why it matters: flammability depends strongly on oxygen concentration and pressure, and exploration habitats are expected to run richer oxygen at lower pressure than the ISS. The ranking shows which microgravity results apply to a given habitat, and where no test covers it. For the planned Moon base, FLEX test #41 ran at 30% O2 and 10.3 psia, while the BASS-II and Saffire solid-material fire tests stopped about 8 oxygen points short. How it works: a Python pipeline reads the 18 PSI experimental-table CSVs, converts every pressure to psia and every O2 value to percent, drops values outside physical bounds as typos, and writes a JSON file with the source file and column of every range. The Next.js (TypeScript) app, deployed on Vercel, ranks investigations by how many values are known, then by the combined relative gap, then by the nearest single test. 35 automated tests (pytest and Vitest) cover the parsing, unit conversion, matching and the data's source quotes. Code: https://github.com/SebAustin/space-apps-2026-flame Limits: O2 and pressure ranges are checked separately; only FLEX, ACME Flame Design and ACME CFI-G list both per test. Ten of the 19 investigations have no O2 or pressure in their PSI table. Partial-gravity data is not in PSI yet. This is a research aid, not a certification tool.
